issues.item: Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not coherent with the stated trauma type. For a relief worker in a war zone, family-related comments could plausibly be relevant, but crash imagery specifically centered on cars hit by accident points toward a road-traffic trauma rather than war-zone relief exposure. The trigger profile therefore mixes two distinct trauma contexts without supporting items linking them.

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies only partially fit the trigger/appraisal pattern. Avoiding social contacts can follow family-related shame or guilt, and avoiding authority figures can fit war-zone exposure, but the set does not clearly connect to the unusual crash-imagery trigger. This makes the coping profile look like it is addressing a different trauma configuration than the trigger items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: Negative appraisals of intrinsic fault and failed role are plausible for a relief worker, but in combination with the crash-accident trigger they create a mismatched formulation: the appraisals imply guilt/responsibility and role failure in humanitarian work, whereas the trigger item implies a motor-vehicle accident trauma. These elements are hard to reconcile as one coherent trauma-linked profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: The trigger profile is not well aligned with the trauma type. For a relief worker in a war zone, police and generic surveillance could be plausible, but recurrent 'cars hit by accident' imagery points toward a road traffic accident trauma rather than war-zone exposure, and no other items anchor this to the stated trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: Avoiding authority figures or uniforms is only weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The trigger item specifies police rather than military, aid command, or armed personnel, making this strategy feel trauma-mismatched for a war-zone relief worker unless other items supported detention, abuse by authorities, or checkpoint-related threat, which they do not.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'There is something about me that made the event happen' is not impossible, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the other selected items. 'Failed Role' fits a relief-worker trauma well, but a strongly self-causal intrinsic blame statement is less coherent without memory or threat content suggesting a specific preventable mistake or personal causation. This creates a mild but meaningful formulation mismatch with the otherwise role-failure/ongoing-reactivity pattern.

vignette: Kiet had been twenty when he deployed to the northern provinces of a fractured country, riding in a white relief convoy tasked with delivering medical supplies to isolated clinics. On the third week, their route crossed a narrow bridge checkpoint manned by armed men in mismatched fatigues. The guards ordered them out of the vehicles, rifles held loose but ready, while Kiet was made to stand under a harsh floodlight, feeling the weight of dozens of eyes tracking his every movement. He spent those hours trying to negotiate passage for a group of displaced families waiting at the end of the road, his voice rising over the tension until his throat gave out. When the situation escalated and the families were turned away, he carried the quiet certainty that his presence had changed nothing. He returned to the United States after his contract ended, holding firmly to the belief that he had failed in his most important role as a relief worker. Back in his home state, Kiet enrolled in a community college to study public health. The campus quickly became a landscape of unspoken threats. He was certain that any security guard walking the quad in a crisp uniform carried the same silent weight he had felt under the checkpoint floodlight, so he began cutting through side alleys to avoid the main administrative building. When a local law enforcement officer directed traffic near his apartment complex, his pulse spiked and his breath caught, the old sensation of being watched closing in. He stopped answering calls from his college friends, avoiding the quiet of his dorm where the faces of people he had socialised with before the war zone would replay in his mind. In conversation, he trained himself never to meet anyone’s eyes, keeping his gaze fixed on the floor or the back of his laptop. Over the months, these choices calcified into habits. He missed a group project deadline because he could not walk past the campus security office without his hands shaking, and he stopped attending a volunteer orientation at a local shelter after seeing an officer escorting a donor vehicle. His body had become a traitor; even sitting in his quiet dorm room, his muscles tightened and his stomach knotted as if he were still standing under that unforgiving light. He had come to believe that his body kept reacting as if he were still in danger, even when he was perfectly safe, and that made resting feel impossible. It was the accumulation of these parallel strains that finally brought Kiet to the university counseling center last Tuesday. He had sat through two full lectures while the campus police conducted a routine training exercise in the courtyard below, forcing himself to remain in his seat as long as he could before the uniform and the radio static pushed him to his feet. He knew he could no longer navigate his classes or his daily routine without constant exhaustion dragging at his shoulders. What frightened him most was the certainty that he would never be able to stop bad things from happening, that every interaction carried the risk of another collapse. He had hoped that stepping into the clinic might at least quiet the relentless scanning of the room and help him remember how to exist in a world that no longer required him to carry the weight of other people’s survival. He was ready to try, as long as it meant he could finally put down the armor he had been wearing for months.
